summary:
Portugal's legal position for transgender visitors is currently permissive. Homosexuality is legal, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010, gender-affirming care is lawful, and legal gender and name change runs under the 2018 self-determination law, which permits self-declaration from age 16 without a medical requirement. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, conversion practices have been banned since 2024, surgery on intersex infants is prohibited, and access to facilities matching a person's gender is protected.

That framework is under active legislative attack. On 20 March 2026 the Assembly of the Republic gave preliminary approval to three bills brought by PSD, Chega and CDS-PP that would reverse the 2018 gender identity law, the first parliamentary vote to roll back self-identification. Reported tallies differ: one account records 124 votes to 79, another 151 to 79. The package was sent to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees. In first reading the bills would reintroduce a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the self-declaration regime available from age 16.

Opposition has been broad. The psychologists' order and trans organisations have described the package as a 'retrocesso' (regression); socialist deputies invoked the 2006 killing of Gisberta, a trans woman murdered by youths in Porto, during the debate, and hundreds protested outside the Assembly. A joint statement by IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal warned that the bills, debated on 19 March and voted on 20 March 2026, would seriously attack trans and intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition; the organisations estimate that adoption would cost Portugal at least four places on the Rainbow Map, dropping it below Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland and France.

The bills also threaten the existing prohibition on forced medical interventions on intersex children, alongside legal gender recognition.

Hate-crime law remains in force. The Penal Code treats sexual orientation and gender identity as explicit grounds for aggravated offences: Articles 132, 144 and 145 aggravate an offence determined by hatred on those grounds, with aggravated assault carrying up to four years, and penalties of one to eight years apply to organising discrimination on those grounds or to genocide-denial-style apology.

Institutional scrutiny of the roll-back is under way. The Ombudsman (Provedoria da Justiça) has requested a constitutional review of Article 176-C of the Penal Code, the provision criminalising acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. A member of the European Parliament has filed written question E-001183/2026 asking the Commission about the repeal process for the 2018 self-determination law and its health and safety impact on trans people.

Take-up of legal gender and name change has risen. Justice Ministry data show changes climbing back toward the high-water mark of two years earlier, with the largest share recorded in Lisbon. The figure is a raw count concentrated in the country's largest city and does not by itself indicate risk.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map 2026 places Portugal 12th at 67%, noting no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban. The score sits below Malta, Iceland and Belgium but above most of Europe.
tangentialFactors:
Public climate indicators include the adoption of 17 May as the National Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia in 2015, annual pride parades in Lisbon and Porto attracting thousands of participants and spectators, and Queer Lisboa, one of Europe's largest LGBT film festivals. Equaldex records high public support for same-sex parenting, ranked first of 30 EU regions.

In 1999 the European Court of Human Rights fined Portugal after a domestic court made homophobic statements in ruling against a gay father's custody of his daughter; the court ruled in the father's favour and ordered custody returned to him.
localsOnly:
Committee-stage analysis by the Commission for Citizenship and Gender Equality warned that the bills would worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people and defended schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties; a Bloco de Esquerda bill was assessed as compatible with school human-rights obligations.

Three draft bills given preliminary approval on 20 March 2026 by 151-79 would ban the inclusion of 'gender ideology' in school curricula; hundreds protested outside the Assembly.

Same-sex couples were barred from adopting and informally forbidden from fostering children until adoption rights took effect on 1 March 2016, after a presidential veto was overridden by Parliament.
outOfScopeNotes:
The three roll-back bills had passed only a first reading and were before the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees; whether they become law, and in what final form, is unresolved in the sources.

Reported vote tallies for the 20 March 2026 approval differ between sources (124-79 and 151-79); the discrepancy is not resolved.

The outcome of the Ombudsman's constitutional review request on Article 176-C is not sourced.

Written question E-001183/2026 is a question; no answer from the Commission is recorded.

Whether the mandatory medical opinion will in fact be reimposed, and from what date, is not established.
